text:
You were fifty-one, and for twenty of those years people called you the man who built half the churches in Kane County. Your company, Rourke & Son Construction. The son was Daniel.

You loved Daniel. You loved him the way you loved the company — as proof you had made something that would outlast you.

In March 2009 your crew hung scaffolding on the Bell Street renovation. Your foreman, Vic Alvarez, told you the ledger boards were split. You were three weeks behind and the client, Pastor Neale, was calling daily. You signed the safety certification yourself — it was Daniel's signature line, but Daniel was at his daughter's christening — and you told Vic the boards would hold until the replacements came Thursday.

They held until Tuesday. Miguel Fuentes, forty-four, a father of three, fell forty feet onto the pavement. He died in the parking lot before the ambulance cleared the siren.

When the investigators came, you said the certification was Daniel's responsibility. You'd been saying you were easing him toward ownership for years; the paperwork, you said, was his job now. You told your wife, Carol, the same thing. You told it so steadily that even Daniel half-believed it — that he'd failed, somehow, through absence, through the christening. He took the plea. Eighteen months.

He came out quiet. In 2014 he parked his truck on the Mill Creek bridge and left the engine running.

You kept the company. You kept going to St. Brigid's. You set up the Fuentes Scholarship at the high school and shook Rosa Fuentes's hand at the banquet where they gave you the Citizen of the Year plaque.

Last February you climbed a ladder in your garage to reach a box of Daniel's things Carol wanted moved out. Your heart stopped on the third rung. The box on the top shelf was labeled in your handwriting: *Bell St. — certification, original.*

You were born second, four minutes after your sister Ruth, and you spent sixty-four years trying to close the gap. Ruth was the one teachers praised. Ruth was the one who got the scholarship to Northwestern. You got pregnant at nineteen by a boy named Kevin who left before Todd was born, and you raised Todd alone on receptionist wages while Ruth traveled for her job in publishing.

Then Ruth brought Howard home for Christmas, 1989. Howard, who laughed with his whole chest. Howard, who noticed you. You told yourself he noticed you too much, and you were right.

You told Howard that Ruth was seeing a married man in Chicago — a fiction you built from a phone number you found on Ruth's dresser. Howard asked Ruth. Ruth denied it. Howard asked you, again, in your kitchen, and you said, "I've never lied to you." It was the first sentence of your marriage. You and Howard married in 1992. Ruth stopped coming to Christmas.

Ruth never married. She drank. She was let go from the publishing house in 2004. She died in 2015 in a rooming house in Rockford, and at the funeral you told everyone she had been troubled since childhood. Howard held your hand. You felt him shaking, and you told yourself it was grief for a sister-in-law.

The lie you lived on: that Howard would have chosen you anyway, that you only saved him from Ruth, that liars get rewarded and you were owed.

Howard died in 2021. Clearing his desk, you found his phone bill from 1989 — the Chicago number, calls to Ruth every Sunday for a year after the wedding. He had known. He had chosen you anyway, and you never learned what to do with that.

Three weeks ago you found Ruth's last letter in the box of her effects. You put it in your coat pocket unopened.

This morning you were holding the letter, the seal still unbroken, when your right hand stopped working.

You are Dana Ruggiero, forty-five, of Toledo, Ohio. You loved your daughter, Maya, who is seventeen and needed tuition for the arts high school — $12,000 a year, money you did not have as a hospital billing clerk.

Your mother, Etta, had $180,000 and Alzheimer's. You held power of attorney. You moved the money into your own account — you told yourself it was temporary, that you were protecting it from her wandering to strangers, that you would pay it back after Maya graduated.

Your brother, Marcus, a machinist in Dayton, never asked for an accounting because he trusted you. You were the good daughter. You drove her to appointments for eleven years, and you let everyone believe that was the whole story.

The memory-care facility at St. Elizabeth's cost $7,200 a month. You said you couldn't afford it. You kept Etta at home instead, alone during your shifts, in a hospital bed in the dining room. You turned down the home aide Marcus offered to split with you, twice. She developed pressure sores, then a urinary tract infection you missed, then sepsis. She died at home on a Tuesday while you were at work reconciling claims.

You told Maya and Marcus and Father Ben at the funeral that the money had gone to Etta's care, every cent. You said it smoothly, and you almost believed it — you had told it to yourself so many times that it had the texture of memory.

Maya found the statements in your filing cabinet looking for the life-insurance paperwork. She stopped speaking to you. She moved in with Marcus. You died five weeks later, at the kitchen table, of a heart attack while filling out the Medicaid application you needed because the estate had nothing left to settle. The denial letter was still in your hand.

You loved your daughter, Lorna, and you loved your friend Ruth Calloway, who hired you to keep the books at the Harbour Street food bank because she said you were the only honest person she knew.

You loved your husband Tom for eleven years, until he left, and after that you loved the balance in your private savings account, which you fed for nine years by moving small amounts — never more than four hundred a month — from the food bank's donations into an account you opened under your maiden name, Eileen Voss.

You told yourself the money was for Lorna. You told yourself donors would waste it anyway. You told yourself that Ruth, who trusted you, would never have to know.

Ruth found the discrepancies in March. She came to your kitchen and put the ledger on the table and said, "Eileen, before I go to the board, tell me it wasn't you." You looked her in the face and said it was Peter Nguyen, the volunteer driver, and you said you'd suspected him for months. You even gave details — his cash box, his trips to the casino in Bathurst.

Peter was charged. Peter had a daughter with epilepsy. Peter lost his licence and his apartment. Ruth visited him in the winter to apologise for doubting him and he told her he forgave her, and she drove home and sat in her garage with the engine running, and the neighbours found her three days later.

You went to Ruth's funeral. You held Ruth's sister's hand. You kept the ledger page in your jewellery box because you couldn't decide whether burning it was safer than keeping it.

You were still deciding when you died, at fifty-seven, of a stroke, in the parking lot of the Bank of Nova Scotia on a Tuesday, with the ledger page in your coat pocket.

You were the one who made it. Out of Millhaven, out of the rented duplex on Kessler Street, out first. That was the whole point of you.

You loved your younger brother, Danny. You loved him the way you loved proof that you were better than where you came from, because Danny stayed, and you left.

In 2008 you owned Kessler Contracting and Danny gave you his retirement — $214,000 — to buy in as your partner. You told him the firm was solid. You told yourself the same thing, every morning, in the truck. The truth was the firm had been bleeding since 2006: two developments in Sadler Township that wouldn't sell, a bank you were slow-rolling, suppliers you were juggling. Danny's money didn't save Kessler Contracting. It paid your mortgage on Halloway Road for three years and the down payment on the boat you named *Second Chance*.

Danny lost the house on Pike Avenue. Marcy divorced him in 2011. He drives a delivery route now, out of the depot on Route 9. At Thanksgiving you carve the turkey and tell the table you did everything you could, that the crash took everyone, that you lost the most.

You want people to see the man who carried the family. The one who bought Mom's wheelchair. The one Danny could always call — though Danny stopped calling in 2013.

The secret is simple: you knew. When Danny signed, you knew the firm was dead, and you let him sign anyway, because his money meant your house, your boat, your face. You chose the face.

In March you drove past the depot on Route 9 and saw Danny loading the truck. You sat in your car in the lot for forty minutes.

You drove home. In the kitchen, reaching for the phone, you felt the crushing weight cross your chest and go down your left arm. You dialed Danny's number and got as far as the area code.
